title: Outfit for the West
premise: Leave town with the right supplies, strong gear, and enough money for the road.

opening.text:
JAUNT: OUTFIT FOR THE WEST. It is sunrise in spring, and the roads west are drying out. Chicago is not the end of your trip. For thousands of people it is a door to the West. Many people passed through town on their way to farms farther west. They came by land and by water, in covered wagons, on horseback and on foot.

You have fifteen dollars and a long way to go. Make your list at the Green Tree inn. Get your harness and iron work checked at Lake and Canal Streets. Then cross the river for food and tools. Spend your money wisely. There are no stores out on the prairie.

stops.text: Start outside the Green Tree, the inn at Lake and West Water Streets. It was named for an oak tree standing close by. Chester Ingersoll ran it from 1834 to 1837. People heading west gather at inns like this one. They share news about the roads and the land offices ahead.
stops.narrative: Make a short list: something to carry your load, a few tools, food for the road and strong iron parts.

stops.text: Walk a block west along Lake Street to Canal Street. In 1833 a shop here sold saddles, harness, horse bridles and trunks. That was the year Silas Cobb came to town. He and his partner split up in February 1835. Cobb says he will keep the shop going. Everything you own has to travel somehow.

choices.label: A pack and straps — $3
choices.consequence: It does not cost much, but you carry the load on your back.

choices.label: Harness mended for a team — $6
choices.consequence: It costs more, but a wagon carries more than you can.

stops.narrative: First decide how your load will travel, or save your money.

stops.text: At the same corner is Asahel Pierce's blacksmith shop. He opened it in October 1833. A history book says he did the iron work for the first stagecoach line from Chicago to St. Louis. Starting in 1834, he also made plows called Bull plows.

choices.label: Have the ironwork checked — $2
choices.consequence: The wheel rims, hooks and chains are checked before the long road.

stops.narrative: Get the iron parts checked before the long road, or trust them as they are.

stops.text: Cross the river to South Water Street. In 1833 a store owned by a man named Jones sold food here. Papers back then said a big barrel of flour cost six dollars. Coffee cost seventeen cents a pound. Tea cost up to a dollar and a quarter a pound. People do not even agree on Jones's first name.

choices.label: Flour, pork and coffee — $5
choices.consequence: Enough food for the first days on the road.

stops.narrative: Stock up now, or plan to buy food along the way.

stops.text: Walk a block east to Peck's store at South Water and LaSalle Streets. His ads from 1833 and 1834 list cloth, tools, food, dishes, boots, shoes and hats.

choices.label: An axe and a few tools — $4
choices.consequence: Tools from the store's shelves, not from the blacksmith's fire.

stops.narrative: Last on your list are tools for the road. Buy some, or trust what you already have.

legs.note: A block west along Lake Street to the Canal Street crossing, where the saddlery's corner is attested and its quadrant is not.
legs.story: Before you buy anything, decide how your load will travel.

legs.note: A few steps: Pierce's documented junction is the same Lake and Canal crossing.
legs.story: Harness and iron parts are both fixed at the same corner.

legs.note: The long leg, and the only crossing: east over the South Branch to the commercial block on South Water Street.
legs.story: Now that you know how to carry it, fill up your load across the river.

endings.text: Every item on your list is crossed off, and your load is packed. You head west ready for the road. You have a little money left, and the town gets smaller and smaller behind you on the flat land.
You set out with a light load, money in your pocket and some things missing. The road will have to give you the rest. But the road does not have many stores.

keepsake.title: Ready for the Road
keepsake.text: A made-up supply list from five Chicago shops, crossed off for the road west.

evidence.text: The Green Tree was a public house at Lake and West Water; the old settlers' account gives Chester Ingersoll as its landlord from 1834 to 1837.
evidence.locator: Inter Ocean, 1 July 1883, 'Old Chicago' early-hotels feature as transcribed by Chicagology; landlord chronology (Ingersoll, 1834–1837).

evidence.text: Goss & Cobb advertised a saddle and harness shop at the corner of Lake and Canal streets, with saddles, harness, bridles, martingales and trunks, and repairs.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 issue, Goss & Cobb advertisement headed 'Saddle & Harness Making', read from the scan.

evidence.text: The Goss & Cobb partnership was dissolved on 18 February 1835, and S. B. Cobb's card printed beside the notice says he will continue the business at his shop.
evidence.locator: 13 June 1835 issue: dissolution notice dated 'Chicago, Feb. 18, 1835' (claim c015) and Cobb's continuation card (claim c016).

evidence.text: P. F. W. Peck advertised from the corner of LaSalle and South Water streets a stock of dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots and shoes, and hats.
evidence.locator: 3 Dec 1833, p. 3, col. 4 (Peck's standing card, run to 10 Dec 1834); 2 July 1834, p. 4, col. 4 ('a full stock of fresh GOODS'). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: A Jones grocery and provision store advertised in 1833; Andreas lists the same trade with forwarding and commission among the 1834 advertisers. The ad reads 'B. Jones', Andreas 'H. Jones'.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 issue, advertisement headed 'Grocery & Provision Store. B. JONES.'; Andreas vol. 1, the 1834 advertisers' summary ('grocery and provision store and forwarding and commission store by H. Jones').

evidence.text: Neither source gives the store's street or lot; its position on South Water Street is a reconstruction.

Asahel Pierce arrived on 8 October 1833 and built a blacksmith shop on Lake Street at the corner of Canal; he ironed the first stage line between Chicago and St Louis in January 1834 and made 'Bull' ploughs from spring 1834.
evidence.locator: Andreas, scan p. 1161, the Asahel Pierce paragraph (arrival, shop at Lake and Canal, Temple & Co. stage-line ironing, the 'Bull' plough).

evidence.text: In 1834 the strangers came 'by land and by water', in prairie schooners and other wagons, 'on horseback and on foot', and 'Many immigrants passed through the town with a view to locating farther west'.
evidence.locator: p. 94, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12724-12751 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The Green Tree was 'so called from an oak tree standing close by', 'one of the most noted in those early days'; it stood until 1880, when it was moved to 33-37 Milwaukee Avenue, 'where it still stands, the oldest memento of early taverns'.
evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98792-98820 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The first numbers of the Democrat, in 1833, quote flour at $6 a barrel, butter at 17 cents a pound, tea at 87 cents to $1.25 a pound, loaf sugar 20 cents, coffee 17, 'whiskey 40 cents a gallon', and calicos 'from 15 to 38 cents' a yard.
evidence.locator: p. 93, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12620-12632 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Immigration in 1833 'assumed proportions surpassing all expectation'; the year's arrivals included John Dean Caton, Silas B. Cobb, Asahel Pierce and the Rev. Jeremiah Porter, and about 165 frame buildings went up.
evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12227-12245 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Each trade is carried to 1 July 1835 from evidence dated before it; none of the sources records a sale, a price or a customer on that day.
evidence.reasoning: Uses the structure records' own scene-date phases: Ingersoll's tenancy spans 1835, Cobb's continuation card runs in June 1835, Peck's card runs to December 1834 and Pierce's shop is attested from 1833 with later enlargement. The Green Tree and Peck positions are inferred; Cobb's and Pierce's corner quadrant is not attested.

evidence.text: The visitor's westward errand, the fifteen-dollar purse, every price, the readiness count, the two endings and the Ready for the Road keepsake are invented connective narrative, not historical events or prices.
